I am thirty-four, but I have been on this land since before I could walk straight. My father needed hands in the field, so I never went past primary school. I started carrying water and seedlings when I was four or five, so forty years feels right. I have 10.1 mu in Quzhou County, and my household has seven mouths—my parents, my wife, my two children, and a younger brother who works construction in Handan when the building season is good. That off-farm money helps, but it means I cannot waste labor on the farm. I drilled a well years ago, and it has saved me from too many dry years.

It is October now, and the maize is harvested and stored. I will put my full 10.1 mu into winter wheat, because that is what this soil knows. I buy improved wheat seed from the township dealer—Lumai or Jinmai, whatever the neighbors trust that year—because the old traditional seeds cannot keep up anymore. I rotary-till the ground after chopping the maize stubble; my small tractor handles it, and I do not have time or extra hands for deep ploughing. At sowing, I spread compound fertilizer, the special kind for wheat with nitrogen and phosphate, about fifty kilograms per mu. Then in spring, when the wheat greens up at jointing, I top-dress with urea. All together that comes to about eighteen kilograms of nitrogen, ten kilograms of phosphorus, and three kilograms of potassium per mu. I irrigate three times using my well: once before winter to help the seedlings survive the frost, once at jointing in March, and once at heading in May. I spray four times total—herbicide early, then insecticide and fungicide when the aphids and rust come with the warm weather. If the frost does not bite too hard, I expect about 500 kilograms per mu.

As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I plant summer maize that same day. There is no time to plough, so I direct-seed with no-tillage using a hybrid variety—Nongda or something similar. The hybrid seed costs more, but it gives me about 550 kilograms per mu. I put down compound fertilizer at sowing and side-dress with a little urea when the maize is knee-high—about twelve kilograms of nitrogen, three kilograms of phosphorus, and three kilograms of potassium per mu total. Maize needs less water than wheat, but August can turn cruel, so I will irrigate twice if the summer rains fail. Three pesticide sprays handle the weeds and corn borers. That is my year. I do not experiment. I do what the land and my father taught me, because my family needs steady grain and steady cash.
